bottom_line: Prices are rising fast again and the economy is running hot, so the Fed (the people who set interest rates) looks set to raise rates again in December. That matters because higher rates make loans, credit cards and mortgages cost more.

stories.title: Inflation hot, Fed likely to hike
stories.real: New Commerce Department data shows inflation and economic growth both running hot. One report puts US inflation at 3.8%, and traders now see the odds of a December Fed rate hike at almost 100%, even with stocks shaky.
stories.you: If the Fed raises rates, borrowing gets more expensive, and that includes credit cards, car loans and new mortgages.

stories.title: Trump calls GDP numbers fake
stories.real: GDP is the total value of everything the country produces. The government revised its third-quarter GDP number sharply higher. President Trump called the data 'fake' and a 'record setting error' and demanded an investigation of the Commerce Department ahead of the midterms.
stories.you: These numbers help decide interest rates, so a fight over whether they can be trusted makes it harder to know where the economy really stands.

stories.title: New tariff threats on 14 countries
stories.real: The US plans a new round of tariffs (taxes on imported goods) on 14 trading partners, and offers lower rates to countries that sign trade deals. Some reports say this makes it more likely the Fed keeps rates higher for longer.
stories.you: Tariffs can push up the prices of imported goods you buy, and they add to the pressure keeping loan rates high.
